note: Texas community-publication supplement only. Five distinct substantive Tribe-published works inspected. No Site, data, build or publication changes; no contact with people or access to citizen-only materials.
minimumCountRecommendation: Five substantive works. The short government roster, archive gateways, service directory, and older constitutional manifestation are excluded from this count. These sources are distinct works, not five independent corroborations of history.

proposedParagraphs.title: A Texas community's account of its past
proposedParagraphs.text: The Tribe's public history places Alabama and Coushatta origins in neighboring areas of what is now Alabama, followed by westward movement into Texas. It connects the Texas community's history with alliances, assistance to refugees during the 1836 conflict and the restoration of federal recognition in 1987. This is the Tribe's concise account of its past. Its references to promised or recognized lands should be read alongside the underlying agreements, rather than converted into a present property map.

proposedParagraphs.title: Different leaders and a shared reservation
proposedParagraphs.text: Chief History separately presents leaders of Alabama villages, Coushatta villages and the later Alabama-Coushatta community. That structure preserves distinctions within a connected history. Its biographies describe Colabe's multilingual interpreting and John Scott's role as a school trustee, linking leadership with diplomacy and education. The introductory settlement account explains how sharing the Polk County reservation encouraged the joint Texas name. It should not be stretched into a claim that all Alabama or Coushatta people everywhere became one government.

proposedParagraphs.title: Constitutional government and cultural responsibilities
proposedParagraphs.text: The July 2023 constitutional consolidation records an original adoption in 1971 and later amendments. It names the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas as the joint legal and governmental unit, then distinguishes chiefs, a seven-member council, administration and courts. Chiefs have cultural, historical and advisory responsibilities; council members serve staggered three-year terms under that text. Its preamble connects self-government with education, language, arts and cultural preservation. These are provisions of this particular Texas government, rather than a constitution for every Alabama person or another nation's institutions.

proposedParagraphs.title: Education, language and women's leadership
proposedParagraphs.text: The Tribal Council's 2023 tribute describes Millie Ann Thompson Williams as the first woman elected to a chief position for the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe. It connects her leadership with a lifetime of Head Start work and identifies her as an Alabama-language teacher and preservation consultant. This public remembrance makes a named educator's contribution visible alongside formal government history. Its account concerns her work and aspirations; it is not evidence of current classroom availability, programme outcomes or a rule about every woman's role.

proposedParagraphs.title: Planning for everyday access
proposedParagraphs.text: The Tribe's April 2025 transportation plan connects infrastructure with the daily needs of residents and visitors. It describes drainage and road-surface problems, coordinating health, education, emergency and transportation departments with external partners. Its strategies include further investigation, seeking funds and developing longer-lasting maintenance solutions. This is a practical example of government planning for community life. The published final draft records goals and a schedule; it does not independently establish that every project was adopted, funded or completed.

integrationNotes: The Alabama entry is broader than this joint Texas Tribe. Keep Alabama people, Coushatta people, the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas government, and Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town distinct. This supplement does not supply evidence about Oklahoma government.
The institutional histories are not independent corroborations of each other or Howard Martin's related Handbook of Texas biographies. The 2014 programme is not an additional counted source.
Use restoration in 1987, not first-ever recognition from the compressed transportation-plan history.
Do not adopt undated officeholders, population/acreage, mutual-intelligibility assertions, or an exact 1836 title effect from these pages.
Chief History's late entries contain chronology inconsistencies; the Millie Williams tribute is a separate dated community work, not a current roster.
Regional associations are broad Texas current/community and Alabama historical/origin associations only. No town pilot, geometry, land-title boundary or all-Indigenous-land claim is supplied.
No archival portraits, ceremonial instructions, worship details or audio were republished. Citizen login and contact routes were not used.
researchGaps: Migration chronology and the legal effect of the 1836/1839 instruments require the separate historical review and primary records.
Later constitutional amendments and implementing ordinances were not reviewed; this is the July 2023 consolidation.
Current teaching provision, learning outcomes and further community voices need separate evidence.
Transportation-plan adoption and implementation require later records rather than inference from its schedule.
Embedded historical books and church records listed by the official-linked archive remain unread leads; archive indexes are not counted as substantive works.
